XIV. SU-ISTAR (235-245)
The texts published here belonged to or concern men called Su-Istar and the
question is whether they refer to the same person and if SO who he was. Both
questions are difficult to answer, because only one text in this chapter mentions the
name of his father, Luzinu. If this is a variant of or mistake for Luzina, we could identify
him as this well-known trader, who occurs a dozen times as father of Su-Istar. In *243
Su-Istar, son of Luzinu, features as the owner of two textiles sold by Liptanum to
Iddin-Assur and he probably kept this document about items he owned. The excavation
number of this text (Kt 91/k 511) does not link it with the group Kt 91/k 534-551, to
which most Su-Istar texts' presented in this chapter belong and in which Su-Istar plays
a role as writer or recipient of letters, creditor or party in a conflict.
Su-Istar was a popular name and in the Kultepe texts there figure at least forty
different Su-Istars. The names of their fathers are usually given in legal documents,
especially when they are witnesses, but we also have witnesses without patronym (e.g.
Su-Istar in *199:19, during eponymy year 94). In Elamma's archive we meet - apart
from the week eponym Su-Istar, son of Assur-bâni, and Su-Istar, the father of the
year-eponym Ennam-Suen (REL 115) - six men whose father is called Su-Istar and at
least five Su-Istars with different fathers; the latter are:
son of Dadanum (see below);
son of Ennam-Assur, *69:24, witness in a debt-note of Elamma;
son of Puzur-Istar, *113:2 with seal B (that mentions the name of his father), an
agreement between him and Elamma, who will send him in Burushattum tin for
which S. will pay him silver; cf. *106:2, which deals with the same transaction;
son of Zu-a-a, *69:36, witness to a debt claim of Elamma;
son of Suk(k)utum, *10:11/*11:8, witness when silver is entrusted for shipment to
Assur.
The first, the son of Dadanum, is the best attested one, also outside our archive. He
features in ATHE 1:1, during the year REL 93, and as witness in three undated records
of Elamma's archive, *15:3, *110:24 (an agreement involving Elamma), and *202:14.
In*3:16 and 22 Elamma is told that this Su-Istar, together with Ennam-Assur, exports
(sesu'um) or bringen (wabalum) merchandise to him, obviously from Assur, where he is
also in *15:3 (as witness) and in AKT 1, 7:25. His role as transporter is confirmed by
TC 3, 26:34, where he will convey messages from Assur to Kanesh, by BIN 4, 13:5-6,
where his seals are on a load of merchandise, and by AKT 6, 865:10-11 (courtesy of
Larsen), where he conducts textiles to Anatolia. According to VS 26, 47:7-8 he ships
silver from Kanesh to Assur, in TC 1, 70:24 he is present there as witness when silver
is entrusted for transport, and in CCT 5, 29a:16-17 he is in Hahhum. He was not only a
transporter, but also himself a trader and Prag I 750:5-6 mentions a debt-note of his for
12 minas of silver.
We already met a Su-Istar in *223, as guarantor of Al-tab, and in the letters
*215-*217 (Ch. XIII) as correspondent of Ennam-Suen. The spelling of these letters, as
pointed out in the introduction to them, shows a few scribal peculiarities, which do not
return in other Su-Istar texts'. Su-Istar also occurs five times as owner of lots of textiles
in the lists presented in Ch. XX (alongside Ennam-Suen, Assur-re'T, and others) and
one of them, *121, deals with textiles owned by him and Ennam-Suen. Important is the

XIV. SU-ISTAR (235-245)
presence in the archive of *151, which lists the expenses of a shipment of merchandise
of Su-Istar, specified on the basis of its "declared value" (awitum; almost 5 talents of
tin, equal to probably three or four donkey-loads of tin and textiles), which indicates that
it was part of a larger, collective caravan (ellutum). It cannot be accidental that *150 is a
very similar record about a shipment of Iddin-Suen, who appears alongside Su-Istar in
several of the textile lists. Something similar may well be the background of *126,
according to which "we I I, Kura and Su-Istar I came together and gave account
(awatam tadanum) to Pilah-Istar, son of Uzua, because of the losses", presumably
suffered by such a caravan. It is not unlikely, though difficult to prove, that the texts of
the present chapter concern this Su-Istar
Texts of Su-Istar in this chapter shed light on his commercial activities and
contacts. Some record debt claims of his, which he would have carefully kept: *241 is a
copy of a debt-note for silver due from Ikunum, with an added memo on various other
debt claims (in all for ca. 110 shekels of silver); *242 a contract for a silver debt
(amount missing) due by IIT-alum, with an agreement on its payment. Text *243 is a
deposition dealing with textiles that belonged to him, and *244 one by witnesses
concerning a private summons, whereby Su-Istar tried to collect a debt of 4 shekels of
gold owed by Puzur-Assur, son of Itur-ill. *235 and *236 are letters of Su-Istar to his
representatives Puzur-Assur and Ikuppi-Assur about an overdue debt of 3 minas of
silver owed by a certain Idnaya; *237 he wrote to Kudadum and two Anatolians. These
letters must be archive copies or they were later returned to him by the addressees. Of
the letters addressed to him *238 (by three men) deals with a large number of textiles
packed in bags, which he "left in the house of Galua"; *239 deals with a possible debt
to Ilis-tikal and *240 with the sale of wool and a silver loan. In the transactions
mentioned in *238 and *240 Pusu-ken is somehow involved and *240:14 mentions an
agreement between Su-Istar and Ir'am-ASsur.
Because it seems rather likely that tablets with consecutive excavation numbers
belonged to one group or file, a few more tablets with numbers between Kt 91/k
534-551 may have belonged to Su-Istar, although this is difficult to prove from their
content. In the letter *273 (Kt 91/545) the name of the addressee is missing, *338 (Kt
91/548) is an anonymous memo in the first person singular, while *299 (Kt 91/k 535)
records a debt owed to "the creditor". This group also comprises some completely
isolated tablets, such as *271 (Kt 91/k 539), a letter from Abduata to Unapse, *263 (Kt
91/k 543) an isolated letter from Sat-Tasmêtim, *267 (Kt 91/k 547) a letter(?) by
Samas-bâni, and *268 (Kt 91/k 550) a letter by Puzur-Ana and Assur-rabi to Su-Belum.
Since it is better to keep separate what cannot be proved to belong together, I did not
include these last texts in this chapter. The just-mentioned four letters figure among the
"Letters from and to various persons" of Ch. XVI; the other texts find their place in Chs.
XIX and XXI.

14-15. The expression "to let somebody drink water" could mean something like "do not

4, 29:44 and Kayseri 293:20-22.

be said to Samas-bani.
Comment
Idnaya might be identical to the man who occurs as debtor of Elamma in
*55:3/"74:6-711"75:5-6 (from eponymy year 81) and *70:29 for some minas of silver, in
*119 settles accounts with him, and in whose caravan Elamma had a share according
to *72:4-5. Su-Istar's polite, but unsuccessful letter to his representatives and Idnaya,
*235, must have been followed by the severe letter *236 to his representatives alone.
How the affair ended remains unknown.

Su-Istar then has to bring her. The information in our letter enables the addressees to
return his debt-note to Huli upon payment.
